member.name: M:ProtoDesigner.Core.Layout.BitMath.MinimumScale(ProtoDesigner.Core.Model.NumericRange,System.Int32)
member.summary: The smallest scale factor that lets fit in bits, i.e. the finest resolution the width can carry: (Max - Min) / (2^bits - 1).
member.remarks: This is the number the editor shows when a user narrows a field's wire size. Pair it with an offset of and the top of the range lands exactly on the largest wire code: a -40..70 temperature in 5 bits gives 110/31 = 3.548..., and (70 - -40) / 3.548... = 31. A larger scale is always legal (coarser, still fits); a smaller one overflows the width.

member.name: M:ProtoDesigner.Core.Layout.BitMath.BitsForScale(ProtoDesigner.Core.Model.NumericRange,System.Decimal)
member.summary: Inverse of : the narrowest width that can carry at the given . Used to tell a user which width their chosen factor implies.

member.name: M:ProtoDesigner.Core.Layout.BitMath.SnapToWholeCode(System.Decimal)
member.summary: Treats a code that sits a hair either side of a whole number as being exactly that number.
member.remarks: returns span / codes rounded to decimal's 28 significant digits. Dividing the span back by that scale therefore lands an ulp above or below codes, and which way it falls is pure luck: 110/255 rounds up, so a -40..70 field in 8 bits reports 255 codes, while 100/255 rounds down, so a 0..100 field in the same 8 bits reports 256 and gets rejected as needing 9. Without this snap the validator refuses the very scale the editor derived for the width the user picked. The tolerance is relative and far below any width a real protocol distinguishes.

member.name: T:ProtoDesigner.Core.Layout.LayoutEngine
member.summary: Computes the wire layout of a message. Stateless and deterministic: the same model always produces the same layout, and no offset is ever stored on the model. Resizing or reordering a field is a model edit followed by a recompute, which is why neither operation needs to "shift" anything.
member.remarks:
Offset conventions:
A node's is relative to the start of its region. A message with no dynamic arrays has exactly one region, so its offsets are absolute.
Struct fields expand inline and carry region-relative offsets.
Nodes beneath an array describe one element and carry element-relative offsets.
Phase 0 limitations, each of which throws rather than producing a wrong answer: an array element must be fixed size, and byte padding requires dynamic element strides to be whole bytes.
